title: Introduction to rfastloess
text: rfastloess high-performance R package LOESS (Locally Weighted Scatterplot Smoothing) built Rust backend. LOESS fits smooth curve scatter plot performing sequence local polynomial regressions. point xix_i, algorithm selects nearest fraction observations, assigns distance-based weights (points farther away receive lower weight), fits weighted least-squares polynomial, reads predicted value xix_i. global model assumed, LOESS adapts naturally non-linear non-stationary data. Optional robustness iterations guard outliers: pass, residuals used recompute per-observation weights high-leverage outliers progressively downweighted. makes iterations > 0 right choice whenever data may contain measurement errors anomalies. Full documentation: https://loess.readthedocs.io/

title: Introduction to rfastloess
code: # From R-universe (pre-built binaries, no Rust required) install.packages("rfastloess", repos = "https://thisisamirv.r-universe.dev")

title: Introduction to rfastloess
text: Loess() accepts smoothing options construction time returns reusable model object. Calling fit(model, x, y) runs algorithm returns LoessResult list. Key result fields $x (input x values), $y (smoothed fitted values), $fraction_used, $iterations_used. fraction parameter controls bandwidth: larger value produces smoother curve cost following local features less closely.
code: library(rfastloess)  # Generate example data set.seed(42) x <- seq(0, 10, length.out = 100) y <- sin(x) + rnorm(100, sd = 0.3)  # Initialize model model <- Loess(fraction = 0.3) print(model) #> <Loess Model> #>   Fraction:          0.3  #>   Iterations:        3  #>   Weight Function:   tricube  #>   Parallel:          TRUE  # Fit model result <- fit(model, x, y) print(result) #> <LoessResult> #>   Points:            100  #>   Fraction Used:     0.3  #>   Iterations Used:   3  # Quick visualization using the S3 plot method plot(result, main = "Auto-plot of LoessResult") # For custom plotting, access components directly plot(x, y, pch = 16, col = "gray", main = "Manual Overlay") lines(result$x, result$y, col = "red", lwd = 2)

title: Introduction to rfastloess
text: Real-world data often contains small fraction gross errors. Setting iterations > 0 activates robustness re-weighting: initial fit, large residuals identify likely outliers contribution downweighted next iteration. bisquare robustness function (default) reduces weight point whose residual exceeds six times median absolute deviation zero. Setting confidence_intervals = 0.95 attaches pointwise 95% confidence bands smoothed curve. reflect uncertainty mean response, individual observations; prediction_intervals provides wider bands covering future observations.
code: # Add outliers y_outliers <- y y_outliers[sample(1:100, 10)] <- y_outliers[sample(1:100, 10)] + 5  # Robust smoothing with confidence intervals result_robust <- fit(Loess(     fraction = 0.3,     iterations = 5,     confidence_intervals = 0.95 ), x, y_outliers)  # Plot plot(x, y_outliers, pch = 16, col = "gray", main = "Robust LOESS") lines(result_robust$x, result_robust$y, col = "red", lwd = 2) lines(result_robust$x, result_robust$confidence_lower, col = "blue", lty = 2) lines(result_robust$x, result_robust$confidence_upper, col = "blue", lty = 2)

title: Introduction to rfastloess
text: return_diagnostics = TRUE, result includes goodness--fit metrics useful comparing different fraction values kernel choices. return_residuals = TRUE attaches raw residuals, return_robustness_weights = TRUE exposes final per-point robustness weights can see observations downweighted.
code:
result_diag <- fit(Loess(     fraction = 0.3,     iterations = 3,     return_diagnostics = TRUE,     return_residuals = TRUE,     return_robustness_weights = TRUE ), x, y)  cat("R-squared:  ", result_diag$r_squared, "
") #> R-squared: cat("RMSE:       ", result_diag$rmse, "
") #> RMSE: cat("MAE:        ", result_diag$mae, "
") #> MAE:  # Residual plot plot(x, result_diag$residuals,     type = "h", col = "steelblue",     main = "Residuals", ylab = "Residual" ) abline(h = 0, lty = 2)

title: Introduction to rfastloess
text: StreamingLoess processes data fixed-size chunks keeps small -memory buffer, making practical datasets otherwise require loading everything RAM . chunk_size parameter controls many observations processed time; chunks stitched together using configurable overlap merge_strategy avoid boundary artefacts. processing chunks, call finalize() retrieve combined LoessResult covering full input range.
code: x_full <- seq(0, 10, length.out = 200) y_full <- sin(x_full) + rnorm(200, sd = 0.2)  model_s <- StreamingLoess(fraction = 0.3, chunk_size = 50L)  # Feed data in chunks of 50 chunk_breaks <- c(0, 50, 100, 150, 200) for (i in seq_len(length(chunk_breaks) - 1)) {     idx <- (chunk_breaks[i] + 1):chunk_breaks[i + 1]     process_chunk(model_s, x_full[idx], y_full[idx]) }  result_s <- finalize(model_s)  plot(x_full, y_full, pch = 16, col = "gray", main = "Streaming LOESS") lines(result_s$x, result_s$y, col = "red", lwd = 2)

title: Introduction to rfastloess
text: OnlineLoess designed real-time data streams observations arrive one time. model maintains sliding window recent window_capacity points. add_point(model, x, y) adds single observation immediately returns smoothed value point - NULL fewer min_points seen yet. update_mode parameter controls window updated: "full" (default) re-smooths window points addition, giving accurate estimate; "incremental" updates newest point, faster less accurate.
code: model_o <- OnlineLoess(     fraction = 0.5,     window_capacity = 30L,     min_points = 3L )  x_stream <- seq(0, 10, length.out = 60) y_stream <- sin(x_stream) + rnorm(60, sd = 0.2)  smoothed_values <- numeric(length(x_stream)) for (i in seq_along(x_stream)) {     out <- add_point(model_o, x_stream[i], y_stream[i])     smoothed_values[i] <- if (is.null(out)) NA_real_ else out$y }  plot(x_stream, y_stream, pch = 16, col = "gray", main = "Online LOESS") lines(x_stream[!is.na(smoothed_values)],     smoothed_values[!is.na(smoothed_values)],     col = "red", lwd = 2 )

title: High-Performance LOESS Smoothing for R
text: implementation robust R’s loess due two key design choices: MAD-Based Scale Estimation: robustness weight calculations, crate uses Median Absolute Deviation (MAD) scale estimation: contrast, R’s loess uses median absolute residuals (MAR): MAD breakdown-point-optimal estimator—remains valid even 50% data outliers. median-centering step removes asymmetric bias residual distributions. MAD provides consistent outlier detection regardless whether residuals centered around zero. Boundary Padding: crate applies range different boundary policies dataset edges: Extend: Repeats edge values maintain local neighborhood size. Reflect: Mirrors data symmetrically around boundaries. Zero: Pads zeros (useful signal processing). NoBoundary: Original Cleveland behavior R’s loess apply boundary padding, can lead : Biased estimates near boundaries due asymmetric local neighborhoods. Increased variance edges smoothed curve.
